events.title: Church of Greece declares autocephaly
events.summary: In the newly independent Kingdom of Greece, the Bavarian regency of King Otto declared the church within the kingdom autocephalous (July 1833), governed by a Holy Synod on the Russian model. Constantinople, still under Ottoman rule, initially regarded the act as uncanonical but recognised the Church of Greece by a Tomos in 1850.
causes: Greek War of Independence (1821–1830)
The new state's unwillingness to leave its church under a patriarch resident in Ottoman Constantinople
Regency adviser Georg von Maurer's state-church design
consequences: Seventeen years of strained relations with the Ecumenical Patriarchate
Tomos of 1850 recognising autocephaly
Pattern of 'national' autocephaly copied across the Balkans

events.title: Ottoman firman creates the Bulgarian Exarchate
events.summary: Under pressure from the Bulgarian national movement, Sultan Abdülaziz issued a firman (1870) creating a Bulgarian Exarchate independent of the Greek-led Patriarchate. A council in Constantinople in 1872 condemned 'ethnophyletism' (organising the church by nationality) and declared the Exarchate schismatic; the schism lasted until 1945.
causes: Bulgarian national revival and resentment of Greek-speaking higher clergy
Ottoman millet politics
Russian diplomatic support
consequences: Schism of 1872–1945 between Constantinople and the Bulgarian church
Condemnation of ethnophyletism (1872), still cited in Orthodox ecclesiology
Restoration of a Bulgarian Patriarchate in 1953 (recognised by Constantinople 1961)

events.title: Constantinople recognises the Romanian Orthodox Church
events.summary: After the union of Moldavia and Wallachia, Prince Alexandru Ioan Cuza's government asserted the independence of the Romanian church (1865). The Ecumenical Patriarchate granted a Tomos of autocephaly in 1885; the church was raised to a patriarchate in 1925.
causes: Union of the Romanian principalities (1859) and independence (1878)
Secularisation of monastic estates (1863) and nationalist church reforms
consequences: Romanian Orthodox autocephaly (1885)
Patriarchate of All Romania (1925)

events.title: Congress of Berat proclaims Albanian Orthodox autocephaly
events.summary: Albanian Orthodox delegates meeting at Berat in September 1922 proclaimed an autocephalous church using the Albanian language, a movement associated with Fan Noli, who had founded Albanian Orthodox parishes in the United States from 1908. Constantinople recognised the autocephaly in 1937.
causes: Albanian independence (1912) and national language movement
Desire for Albanian-language liturgy instead of Greek
consequences: Recognition by Constantinople (1937)
Church suppressed when Albania declared itself an atheist state (1967)
Rebuilt after 1991 under Archbishop Anastasios (Yannoulatos)

events.title: Tomos of autocephaly for the Polish Orthodox Church
events.summary: With most of its faithful Belarusian and Ukrainian inhabitants of the restored Polish state, the Orthodox Church in Poland received a Tomos of autocephaly from Constantinople in November 1924. The Moscow Patriarchate did not accept it, and granted its own act of autocephaly in 1948 after Poland entered the Soviet sphere.
causes: Restoration of Polish independence (1918)
Polish government's wish to sever the church from Moscow
Collapse of the pre-revolutionary Russian church order
consequences: Rival canonical narratives (1924 vs 1948) about the source of autocephaly
Precedent later cited in the Ukrainian dispute

events.title: Russian Church Abroad organised in exile
events.summary: Russian bishops evacuated with the White armies formed a Supreme Church Administration Abroad in Constantinople (November 1920), citing Patriarch Tikhon's decree no. 362 permitting dioceses cut off from Moscow to govern themselves. In 1921 it moved to Sremski Karlovci in Serbia, where an all-diaspora council met.
events.longText: The Synod moved from Sremski Karlovci (Serbia) to Munich after the Second World War and to New York in 1950. Its relationship with Moscow was broken for most of the Soviet period; it canonised the New Martyrs of Russia in 1981. On 17 May 2007, Metropolitan Laurus and Patriarch Alexy II signed the Act of Canonical Communion, making ROCOR a self-governing part of the Moscow Patriarchate; a minority of clergy and parishes refused the union.
causes: Russian Civil War and emigration of over a million Russians
Bolshevik persecution and the isolation of Patriarch Tikhon
consequences: Formation of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia (ROCOR)
Rejection of Metropolitan Sergius's 1927 declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state
Act of Canonical Communion with the Moscow Patriarchate (2007)

events.title: Moscow grants autocephaly to the Orthodox Church in America
events.summary: In April 1970 the Moscow Patriarchate granted autocephaly to the former Russian Orthodox 'Metropolia' in North America, which took the name Orthodox Church in America. The Ecumenical Patriarchate and several other churches did not recognise the act, holding that only Constantinople may grant autocephaly in the diaspora.
causes: Decades of separation between the American Metropolia and Moscow after 1917
Desire for a single, local, English-speaking American Orthodox church
consequences: Recognition by Moscow and some churches (e.g. Bulgaria, Georgia, Poland, Czech Lands and Slovakia) but not by Constantinople
Ongoing debate over 'diaspora' jurisdiction and canonical territory

events.title: Eritrean Orthodox Church separates from the Ethiopian church
events.summary: After Eritrea's independence from Ethiopia (1993), the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate under Pope Shenouda III agreed to the Eritrean church's autocephaly; Abune Philipos was consecrated as first Patriarch of Eritrea in Cairo in 1998.
causes: Eritrean war of independence (1961–1991) and independence referendum (1993)
Desire for a national church distinct from the Ethiopian Patriarchate
consequences: Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church established
Strained relations with the Ethiopian Orthodox Church
Later state involvement in the deposition of Patriarch Antonios (2006)

events.title: Catholicate established in Malankara; Orthodox–Jacobite division
events.summary: After Patriarch Abdullah II of the Syriac Orthodox Church excommunicated Metropolitan Vattasseril Geevarghese Mar Dionysius (1911), his party invited the earlier-deposed Patriarch Abdul Masih II, who consecrated a Catholicos for the East in Malankara in 1912. The church divided between those who stressed Malankara autonomy (later the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church) and those who stressed obedience to the Patriarch of Antioch (the Jacobite Syrian Christian Church).
causes: Disputes over control of church property and the authority of the Antiochene patriarch in India
Indian Christian self-assertion under colonial rule
consequences: Two parties ('Methran' and 'Bava' factions) and decades of litigation
Reunion in 1958 after a Supreme Court of India ruling; renewed division from 1975
Supreme Court judgement of 2017 holding the 1934 constitution binding on parishes, followed by disputes over church buildings

events.title: Royal Court verdict and the formation of the Mar Thoma Church
events.summary: Reform among the St Thomas Christians, led from 1836 by Abraham Malpan of Maramon and encouraged by contact with Church Missionary Society missionaries, revised the Syriac liturgy to remove prayers for the dead and the invocation of saints. When the Royal Court of Travancore ruled in 1889 that church property belonged to the party loyal to the Syriac patriarch, the reform party continued as the Mar Thoma Syrian Church.
causes: CMS 'Mission of Help' (from 1816) and the Malayalam Bible
Abraham Malpan's liturgical reforms (1836)
Contest between Mathews Mar Athanasius and the patriarchal party over the metropolitanate
consequences: Mar Thoma Syrian Church as an Oriental-rite church with Reformation emphases
Maramon Convention (from 1895)
Later communion relations with Anglican churches and the Church of South India

events.title: Catholicosate restored at Etchmiadzin; Cilician line continues at Sis
events.summary: The supreme Armenian see had followed the Armenian kingdom to Cilicia, residing at Sis from 1293. In 1441 an assembly at Etchmiadzin elected a new Catholicos there, while the Catholicos at Sis continued his own line, creating the two Catholicosates of All Armenians (Etchmiadzin) and of the Great House of Cilicia.
causes: Fall of the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia (1375)
Desire to return the patriarchal seat to historic Armenia
consequences: Two catholicosates sharing one faith and liturgy
Cilician see moved to Antelias, Lebanon, in 1930 after the genocide

events.title: Consecration of Mar Thoma Darmo and the Ancient Church of the East
events.summary: Opposition to Patriarch Mar Eshai Shimun XXIII's adoption of the Gregorian calendar (1964) and to hereditary patriarchal succession led a party in Iraq to consecrate Mar Thoma Darmo, metropolitan in India, as a rival patriarch in Baghdad in 1968.
causes: Calendar reform of 1964
Long-standing objections to uncle-to-nephew patriarchal succession
Patriarch's residence in exile in the United States
consequences: Ancient Church of the East with a Baghdad-based patriarchate
Ongoing reconciliation talks with the Assyrian Church of the East

events.title: Yohannan Sulaqa consecrated in Rome: origin of the Chaldean Catholic Church
events.summary: In 1552 opponents of hereditary patriarchal succession in the Church of the East elected Yohannan Sulaqa, abbot of Rabban Hormizd monastery, who travelled to Rome and was consecrated patriarch by Pope Julius III in 1553. Sulaqa was killed in 1555; after a complex history of shifting lines, a single Catholic 'Patriarchate of Babylon of the Chaldeans' was consolidated in 1830 under Yohannan Hormizd.
causes: Hereditary succession within one patriarchal family
Catholic missionary contacts and Ottoman–Safavid politics
consequences: Rival patriarchal lines (Eliya and Shimun) for three centuries
Chaldean Catholic Church formally consolidated in 1830
Patriarchal seat moved to Baghdad in 1950

events.title: Disputed patriarchal election divides the Church of Antioch
events.summary: On the death of Patriarch Athanasius III Dabbas, the pro-Catholic party in Damascus elected Cyril VI Tanas, while Constantinople consecrated the Athonite monk Sylvester. Rome recognised Cyril in 1729; his followers became the Melkite Greek Catholic Church and Sylvester's the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch.
causes: Decades of Catholic missionary activity in Aleppo and Damascus
Rivalries between Damascus and Aleppo elites
Ottoman recognition politics
consequences: Two Byzantine-rite churches in the Antiochian patriarchate
Melkite civil recognition by the Ottomans (1848)

events.title: Union of Uzhhorod
events.summary: Sixty-three Orthodox priests of the Mukachevo region of Habsburg Hungary professed union with Rome in the castle chapel of Uzhhorod (24 April 1646), keeping their Byzantine liturgy and married clergy. It is the founding act of the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church.
causes: Habsburg and Counter-Reformation support for church union
Hopes of equal status and privileges with Latin clergy
consequences: Mukachevo Greek Catholic eparchy (1771)
Soviet liquidation of the church in 1949 and revival in 1989
Ruthenian emigration to the United States

events.title: Mar Ivanios enters Catholic communion
events.summary: On 20 September 1930 Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios, founder of the Bethany monastic movement, and Bishop Jacob Mar Theophilos of the Malankara Orthodox church were received into communion with Rome while keeping the West Syriac liturgy, creating the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church.
causes: Malankara Orthodox–Jacobite divisions after 1912
Ecumenical overtures from Rome on condition of retaining the Antiochene rite
consequences: Syro-Malankara Catholic hierarchy (1932)
Major archiepiscopal status (2005)

events.title: Founding of the Polish National Catholic Church
events.summary: Polish immigrant parishioners in Scranton, at odds with their Irish-American bishop over parish property and Polish-led leadership, organised St Stanislaus parish under Fr Francis Hodur (1897). Hodur was excommunicated in 1898 and consecrated a bishop by Old Catholic bishops in Utrecht in 1907.
causes: Trustee and property disputes in immigrant parishes
Polish national feeling and resentment of non-Polish hierarchy
consequences: Polish National Catholic Church with mission in Poland
Membership of the Old Catholic Union of Utrecht (1907–2003)
Dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church from the 1980s

events.title: Écône consecrations
events.summary: On 30 June 1988 Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, founder of the Society of St Pius X, consecrated four bishops without papal mandate. The Holy See declared that Lefebvre and the four bishops had incurred excommunication and described the act as schismatic; the Society maintained that a state of necessity justified it in order to preserve Catholic tradition.
causes: Opposition to aspects of Vatican II (religious liberty, ecumenism, collegiality) and to the 1969 Mass of Paul VI
Failed 1988 protocol between Lefebvre and Cardinal Ratzinger
consequences: Motu proprio Ecclesia Dei (1988) and the founding of the Priestly Fraternity of St Peter
Remission of the four bishops' excommunications by Benedict XVI (2009)
Continuing doctrinal talks without full canonical regularisation

events.title: Proclamation of the Iglesia Filipina Independiente
events.summary: On 3 August 1902 labour leader Isabelo de los Reyes proclaimed an independent Filipino church at a meeting of the Unión Obrera Democrática, naming the priest Gregorio Aglipay as its head. It arose from nationalist resentment of Spanish friar control during the Philippine Revolution.
causes: Philippine Revolution (1896–1898) and anti-friar nationalism
Rome's refusal to appoint Filipino bishops quickly
consequences: A large secession of Filipino Catholics in the early 1900s
Supreme Court ruling (1906) returning occupied church buildings to the Catholic Church
Concordat of full communion with the Episcopal Church (1961)

events.title: Riksdag of Västerås
events.summary: King Gustav Vasa's diet at Västerås transferred church property and jurisdiction to the crown and permitted evangelical preaching, beginning the Swedish Reformation. The Lutheran character of the Church of Sweden was confirmed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, which adopted the Augsburg Confession.
causes: Royal need for revenue after independence from the Kalmar Union
Evangelical preaching of Olaus and Laurentius Petri
consequences: Church of Sweden under royal authority
Swedish Bible (1541)
Uppsala Synod (1593)

events.title: Danish–Norwegian Church Ordinance
events.summary: After his victory in the civil war (the Count's Feud), Christian III arrested the Catholic bishops (1536) and introduced a Lutheran Church Ordinance (1537), drafted with Johannes Bugenhagen, for Denmark and Norway; it was formally applied in Norway in 1539.
causes: Count's Feud (1534–36)
Royal appropriation of church lands
Wittenberg influence
consequences: Lutheran state churches of Denmark, Norway and Iceland
Superintendents (later bishops) appointed by the crown

events.title: Prussian Union of Churches
events.summary: For the 300th anniversary of the Reformation, King Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia, himself Reformed while most subjects were Lutheran, called for Lutheran and Reformed congregations to unite in one Evangelical church; a common agenda (liturgy) followed in 1822. Friedrich Schleiermacher supported union in principle while criticising royal control of worship.
causes: Reformation tercentenary (1817)
Enlightenment and Pietist weariness with confessional division
Royal family's Reformed confession
consequences: Union churches in Prussia and other German states
Resistance and emigration of 'Old Lutherans' to North America and Australia
Basis of today's member churches of the EKD and the Union of Evangelical Churches

events.title: Founding of the Missouri Synod
events.summary: German Lutheran pastors, including Saxon immigrants led by C. F. W. Walther and missionaries sent by Wilhelm Löhe, organised 'The German Evangelical Lutheran Synod of Missouri, Ohio, and Other States' at Chicago in April 1847.
causes: Saxon emigration of 1838–39 seeking confessional freedom
Opposition to the Prussian Union and to 'American Lutheranism'
consequences: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod (name from 1947)
Network of parochial schools and Concordia seminaries
1974 'Seminex' walkout over biblical interpretation

events.title: Constituting convention of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America
events.summary: The American Lutheran Church, the Lutheran Church in America and the Association of Evangelical Lutheran Churches merged at a constituting convention in Columbus, Ohio (1987); the new church began operating on 1 January 1988.
causes: Twentieth-century Lutheran merger movement
Departure of moderates from the Missouri Synod in the 1970s
consequences: Largest Lutheran church in the United States
Full-communion agreements with Reformed, Episcopal, Moravian and Methodist churches (1997–2009)
Departure of congregations to the LCMC and NALC after 2009 decisions on sexuality

events.title: Founding of the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus
events.summary: Congregations founded by Scandinavian, German and American Lutheran missions, together with Ethiopian evangelical believers, united as an autonomous national church in January 1959, taking the name of the Addis Ababa congregation 'Mekane Yesus' ('Place of Jesus').
causes: Growth of evangelical congregations especially in western and southern Ethiopia
Missions' commitment to an autonomous Ethiopian church
consequences: Rapid growth into one of the world's largest Lutheran churches
Persecution under the Derg; murder of General Secretary Gudina Tumsa (1979)
Union with the Bethel (Presbyterian) synod (1974)

events.title: Missionary conference at Sipirok and the beginning of the HKBP
events.summary: On 7 October 1861 Rhenish Mission missionaries meeting at Sipirok agreed to work among the Batak of North Sumatra, the date the Huria Kristen Batak Protestan counts as its founding. Ludwig Ingwer Nommensen, arriving in 1862, led the mission into the Silindung valley and Lake Toba region.
causes: Rhenish Mission strategy in Sumatra
Earlier failed missions (e.g. the killing of Lyman and Munson, 1834)
consequences: Mass conversion of the Toba Batak
Church order granting autonomy (1930) and first Batak ephorus (1940)
HKBP Confession of Faith (1951)

events.title: Laestadius's awakening at Karesuando
events.summary: Lars Levi Laestadius, Lutheran pastor and botanist at Karesuando in Swedish Lapland, experienced a spiritual awakening in 1844, which he attributed to a conversation with a Sami woman, Milla Clementsdotter. His preaching sparked a revival among Sami, Finnish and Swedish people of the far north.
causes: Alcohol abuse and poverty in the north
Earlier Pietist awakenings in the Nordic countries
consequences: Laestadian movement within the Nordic Lutheran churches
Emigration of Laestadians to North America and later divisions into several branches

events.title: Scottish Reformation Parliament
events.summary: In August 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction, forbade the Mass and approved the Scots Confession drafted by John Knox and five colleagues. The First Book of Discipline (1560) and later Andrew Melville's Second Book of Discipline (1578) shaped a Presbyterian church order.
causes: Lords of the Congregation's rebellion against Mary of Guise
English intervention and the Treaty of Edinburgh (1560)
Knox's return from Geneva (1559)
consequences: Reformed national Church of Scotland
A century of conflict between Presbyterian and episcopal church government
Presbyterian settlement of 1690

events.title: Disruption of 1843
events.summary: On 18 May 1843 about a third of the ministers of the Church of Scotland, led by Thomas Chalmers, walked out of the General Assembly and formed the Free Church of Scotland, giving up their stipends and manses. They protested that civil courts and lay patrons were overriding the church's spiritual independence in appointing ministers.
causes: Patronage Act of 1712 allowing patrons to present ministers
The 'Ten Years' Conflict' and court rulings against the Veto Act (1834)
Evangelical party's doctrine of the 'Crown Rights of the Redeemer'
consequences: Free Church of Scotland and a vast church-building and school programme
Abolition of patronage (1874)
Reunions of 1900 (United Free Church) and 1929 (with the Church of Scotland)
Church of Scotland Act 1921 recognising spiritual independence

events.title: Synod of Emden
events.summary: Exiled Dutch Reformed congregations meeting at Emden in East Frisia (October 1571) adopted a Presbyterian-synodal order and the Belgic and Heidelberg confessions, laying the foundations of the Dutch Reformed Church.
causes: Spanish persecution in the Netherlands
Refugee churches in Emden, London and the Rhineland
consequences: Reformed public church of the Dutch Republic
Framework later confirmed at the Synod of Dort (1618–19)

events.title: Synod of Debrecen
events.summary: A synod at Debrecen under Péter Méliusz Juhász adopted the Second Helvetic Confession, marking the consolidation of a Reformed church among Hungarian speakers; the Heidelberg Catechism also became a standard. Debrecen came to be called 'the Calvinist Rome'.
causes: Spread of Swiss Reformed theology in Ottoman-divided Hungary and Transylvania
Antitrinitarian controversy in Transylvania
consequences: Reformed Church in Hungary
Reformed colleges at Debrecen and Sárospatak

events.title: Secession of 1857 and the Christian Reformed Church
events.summary: In 1857 several congregations of Dutch immigrants in west Michigan left the Reformed Protestant Dutch Church (today's Reformed Church in America), objecting to its Americanised practices such as hymn singing, open communion and tolerance of Freemasonry. They formed what became the Christian Reformed Church.
causes: Heritage of the 1834 Afscheiding (Secession) in the Netherlands
Suspicion of American revivalism and lodge membership
consequences: Christian Reformed Church in North America
Calvin College and Seminary (Grand Rapids)
Strong Kuyperian Christian school movement

events.title: Reunion forming the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)
events.summary: The northern United Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. and the southern Presbyterian Church in the United States, divided since the Civil War (1861), reunited at a General Assembly in Atlanta in June 1983.
causes: Civil War and slavery-era division of American Presbyterianism
Decline of sectional identity and ecumenical commitments
consequences: Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), headquartered in Louisville
Some conservative congregations moved to the PCA or the EPC

events.title: First General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America
events.summary: Conservative congregations leaving the southern Presbyterian Church in the United States held their first General Assembly at Briarwood Presbyterian Church, Birmingham, in December 1973, citing theological liberalism, women's ordination and a planned merger with the northern church.
causes: Disputes over biblical inerrancy and the Westminster Standards
Opposition to union with the UPCUSA
consequences: Presbyterian Church in America
Joining and receiving of the Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod (1982)

events.title: Division of the Presbyterian Church of Korea (Tonghap and Hapdong)
events.summary: At its 44th General Assembly in Daejeon (1959) the Presbyterian Church of Korea divided into the Tonghap ('united') and Hapdong ('joint') denominations. The disputes centred on membership in the World Council of Churches, theological direction and a controversy over a seminary land purchase.
causes: Earlier splits over the Shinto shrine issue (Kosin, 1952) and biblical criticism (Kijang, 1953)
Cold War suspicion of ecumenism
Regional and institutional rivalries
consequences: Two large Presbyterian denominations of comparable size
Proliferation of further Korean Presbyterian bodies

events.title: First national synod of the French Reformed churches
events.summary: Delegates of French Reformed congregations met secretly in Paris in May 1559 and adopted a confession of faith (the Gallican Confession, revised at La Rochelle in 1571) and a discipline establishing consistories and synods.
causes: Rapid growth of Reformed churches under Genevan influence
Persecution under Henri II
consequences: Organised Huguenot church
French Wars of Religion (1562–1598)
Edict of Nantes (1598)

events.title: First Zurich Disputation
events.summary: In January 1523 the Zurich council heard Huldrych Zwingli defend his Sixty-Seven Articles against the bishop of Constance's representatives and authorised him to continue preaching from Scripture, launching the Reformation in Zurich.
causes: Zwingli's biblical preaching from 1519
Lenten sausage affair (1522)
Civic control of religion in Swiss cities
consequences: Abolition of the Mass in Zurich (1525)
Spread to Bern (1528), Basel and other cities
Second Helvetic Confession (1566)

events.title: Abolition of episcopacy in the Church of Scotland
events.summary: After the Revolution of 1688, the Scottish bishops refused to swear allegiance to William and Mary. Parliament abolished episcopacy in 1689 and re-established Presbyterian government in 1690; the episcopalian clergy and laity who remained loyal formed what became the Scottish Episcopal Church.
causes: Glorious Revolution of 1688
Jacobite loyalty of the bishops
Long Presbyterian–episcopal struggle since 1560
consequences: Nonjuring Scottish Episcopal Church, under penal laws especially after 1746
Consecration of Samuel Seabury for America (1784)

events.title: General Convention constitutes the Episcopal Church
events.summary: After American independence, Samuel Seabury was consecrated bishop by Scottish nonjuring bishops in Aberdeen (1784), and William White and Samuel Provoost by English bishops (1787). The General Convention of 1789 in Philadelphia adopted a constitution and an American Book of Common Prayer for the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States.
causes: American Revolution and the end of the Church of England's colonial role
Need for bishops without an oath to the British crown
consequences: First autonomous Anglican church outside the British Isles
Model of synodical government with lay participation

events.title: Inauguration of the Province of Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi
events.summary: The Anglican dioceses of Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, rooted in the Church Missionary Society mission begun in 1877, became a self-governing province in 1961, with Leslie Brown as first archbishop; Erica Sabiti became the first African archbishop in 1966.
causes: Growth of the CMS church and the East African Revival (from the 1930s)
Decolonisation
consequences: Church of Uganda
Archbishop Janani Luwum's murder under Idi Amin (1977)

events.title: Church of the Province of Kenya inaugurated
events.summary: The Anglican dioceses of Kenya, part of the Province of East Africa from 1960, became the separate Church of the Province of Kenya in 1970, with Festo Olang' as archbishop. It was renamed the Anglican Church of Kenya in 1998.
causes: CMS mission begun by Johann Ludwig Krapf at Mombasa (1844)
Kenyan independence (1963)
consequences: Anglican Church of Kenya
Prominent role in Kenyan public life and in GAFCON

events.title: Church of Nigeria becomes a separate province
events.summary: The Nigerian dioceses of the Church of the Province of West Africa (formed 1951) became the separate Church of Nigeria in 1979, building on the CMS mission begun at Badagry and Abeokuta in the 1840s and the episcopate of Samuel Ajayi Crowther.
causes: Growth of Nigerian Anglicanism
Desire for a national province
consequences: Rapid growth in the 'Decade of Evangelism' (1990s)
Leadership in the GAFCON movement from 2008

events.title: Formation of the Anglican Church in North America
events.summary: At an assembly in Bedford, Texas, in June 2009, dioceses and congregations that had left the Episcopal Church and the Anglican Church of Canada, together with older continuing bodies such as the Reformed Episcopal Church, formed the Anglican Church in North America under Archbishop Robert Duncan.
causes: Consecration of a partnered gay bishop (2003) and same-sex blessings
Disputes over biblical authority
GAFCON's Jerusalem Declaration (2008)
consequences: ACNA recognised by GAFCON primates but not a member of the Anglican Communion's formal structures
Extensive property litigation with the Episcopal Church

traditions.name: Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople
traditions.summary: The see of Constantinople (Istanbul), whose bishop was ranked second after Rome by the Council of Constantinople (381) and given wide jurisdiction by canon 28 of Chalcedon (451). Since 1054 it has been regarded by the Orthodox as 'first among equals' among autocephalous churches. Its direct flock in Turkey is small, but it oversees Mount Athos, Crete and the Dodecanese, the autonomous churches of Finland and Estonia and many diaspora dioceses, including the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America.
distinctives: Primacy of honour ('first among equals') among Orthodox churches
Claimed right to grant autocephaly and hear appeals (contested by Moscow)
Spiritual centre at the Phanar in Istanbul
Jurisdiction over much of the diaspora under canon 28 of Chalcedon
Leading role in ecumenism and environmental theology ('the Green Patriarch')

traditions.status: Active. The Halki theological school has been closed by Turkish law since 1971. Relations with Moscow were broken after Constantinople's 2018–19 Ukrainian decision.

traditions.name: Church of Greece
traditions.summary: The autocephalous Orthodox church of the Greek state, declared independent of Constantinople in 1833 and recognised by the Ecumenical Patriarchate's Tomos of 1850. The Greek constitution names Eastern Orthodoxy the 'prevailing religion'. Metropolises of the 'New Lands' annexed after 1912 are administered by the Church of Greece while remaining canonically under Constantinople; Crete and the Dodecanese stay with the Patriarchate.
distinctives: National church closely tied to Greek identity and state
Holy Synod presided over by the Archbishop of Athens
Strong monastic culture, including Meteora
Recognised the Orthodox Church of Ukraine in 2019
Mount Athos remains under Constantinople, not Athens

traditions.name: Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch and All the East
traditions.summary: The Chalcedonian (Byzantine-rite) Patriarchate of Antioch, claiming foundation by the apostles Peter and Paul, whose seat has been in Damascus since the fourteenth century. After the separation of the non-Chalcedonian Syriac Orthodox line (6th century), it became the church of the Arabic-speaking 'Rum' Orthodox of Syria and Lebanon. Since 1899 its patriarchs have been Arabs. A large emigrant church exists in the Americas and Australia.
distinctives: Arabic-language Byzantine Orthodoxy (the 'Rum Orthodox')
Seat in Damascus; Balamand as theological centre
Antiochian Orthodox Archdiocese of North America, with a Western Rite vicariate
Strong presence in Latin America through Levantine emigration
Suffering and displacement in the Syrian war (from 2011)

traditions.name: Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa
traditions.summary: The Chalcedonian Patriarchate of Alexandria, which after 451 was a minority beside the Coptic Orthodox Church. Long the church of Greek communities in Egypt, in the twentieth century it gained a large African flock, beginning with the movement of Reuben Spartas in Uganda (1920s–1940s), and now has dioceses across sub-Saharan Africa.

Jurisdiction over the whole of Africa
Rapid growth through African mission (Kenya, Uganda, DR Congo, etc.)
Recognised the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (2019), after which Moscow created a rival African exarchate (2021)

traditions.name: Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem
traditions.summary: Raised to patriarchal rank at the Council of Chalcedon (451), the Patriarchate of Jerusalem is custodian, with the Latins and Armenians, of the principal Holy Places under the Ottoman 'Status Quo' arrangements. Its hierarchy is drawn largely from the Greek Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, while most of its faithful are Arabic-speaking Palestinians and Jordanians — a long-standing source of tension. The autonomous Archdiocese of Sinai (St Catherine's Monastery) is connected with it.
distinctives: Guardian of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Bethlehem's Church of the Nativity
Holy Fire ceremony on Holy Saturday
Greek-led hierarchy and Arab laity
Ottoman-era Status Quo regulating shared holy sites

traditions.status: Active in Israel, the Palestinian territories and Jordan; disputes over church land sales have caused controversy.

traditions.name: Serbian Orthodox Church
traditions.summary: Founded as an autocephalous archbishopric by St Sava in 1219, raised to a patriarchate at Peć in 1346, abolished by the Ottomans in 1766 and restored as a unified patriarchate in 1920. It is closely bound to Serbian national memory, including the Kosovo tradition, and suffered heavily in the Second World War and under communism.
distinctives: St Sava's foundation and the 'Svetosavlje' ideal
Medieval monasteries in Kosovo (Dečani, Peć, Gračanica)
Patriarchate restored 1920
Recognised the Archbishopric of Ohrid (North Macedonia) in 2022, ending a long dispute
Disputes with the Montenegrin Orthodox movement

profile.canon: Old Testament from the Septuagint, including the books Protestants call deuterocanonical (anagignoskomena), and the 27-book New Testament.

traditions.status: Active; the majority church of Serbia and the Republika Srpska.

traditions.name: Romanian Orthodox Church
traditions.summary: The Orthodox church of the Romanian people, the only large Orthodox church of Latin language and culture. Autocephalous since 1885 and a patriarchate since 1925, it survived communist control (1947–1989) with both compromise and martyrdom, and has grown institutionally since 1989, including a large diaspora in Italy and Spain.
distinctives: Latin-language Orthodox culture
Painted monasteries of Bukovina
Philokalic revival (Dumitru Stăniloae's Romanian Philokalia)
Cathedral of the Nation's Salvation in Bucharest (consecrated 2018)
Large Western European diaspora

traditions.name: Bulgarian Orthodox Church
traditions.summary: The church that grew from the baptism of Khan Boris I (864) and the Slavonic literary school of Clement and Naum of Ohrid. A Bulgarian patriarchate existed in the medieval tsardoms; under the Ottomans it was absorbed into the Greek-led patriarchate. The Exarchate of 1870 led to a schism with Constantinople (1872–1945). The patriarchate was restored in 1953.

Rila Monastery and St John of Rila
Condemnation of its 1870 Exarchate as 'ethnophyletism' (1872)
Internal schism of 1992–2010 related to communist-era appointments

traditions.name: Georgian Orthodox Church
traditions.summary: Rooted in the conversion of King Mirian III through St Nino (c. 337), the Georgian church became autocephalous under a Catholicos in late antiquity. Russia abolished its autocephaly in 1811; it was restored in 1917, recognised by Moscow in 1943 and by Constantinople in 1990. Under Patriarch Ilia II (from 1977) it has become Georgia's most trusted institution.
distinctives: St Nino's grapevine cross
Distinctive Georgian polyphonic chant
Ancient Georgian script and liturgical tradition
Strong identification with Georgian national identity

traditions.name: Church of Cyprus
traditions.summary: The church of Cyprus traces its origin to the mission of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13). The Council of Ephesus (431) upheld its independence from Antioch, and Emperor Zeno later confirmed its privileges after the discovery of the relics of Barnabas — including the archbishop's right to sign in red ink. Under Ottoman rule the archbishop became ethnarch of the Greek Cypriots; Archbishop Makarios III became the first president of the Republic of Cyprus (1960).

Archbishop's imperial privileges (red ink, sceptre, purple cloak)
Ethnarchic political role
Churches in the north affected by the division of the island since 1974

traditions.name: Polish Autocephalous Orthodox Church
traditions.summary: The Orthodox church of Poland, drawing its members mainly from Belarusian, Ukrainian and Lemko minorities. Constantinople granted autocephaly in 1924; Moscow, which did not accept that act, issued its own grant in 1948. Its centre is in Warsaw, with a historic heartland in the Podlasie region around Białystok.
distinctives: Minority church in a majority-Catholic country
Pilgrimage to the Holy Mountain of Grabarka
Disputed origin of autocephaly (1924 vs 1948)
Did not recognise the Orthodox Church of Ukraine

traditions.name: Orthodox Autocephalous Church of Albania
traditions.summary: The Albanian Orthodox church proclaimed autocephaly at the Congress of Berat (1922) and was recognised by Constantinople in 1937. When Enver Hoxha declared Albania an atheist state (1967) all religious practice was banned and clergy imprisoned or killed. From 1992 Archbishop Anastasios (Yannoulatos), a Greek missiologist appointed by Constantinople, rebuilt the church almost from nothing, until his death in 2025.

Survival through total state prohibition (1967–1990)
Post-communist reconstruction: seminary, hospitals, schools
Ministry in a religiously mixed Muslim–Christian society

traditions.name: Orthodox Church in America
traditions.summary: Descended from the Russian mission to Alaska begun by Valaam monks in 1794 (St Herman of Alaska), the diocese moved to San Francisco (1872) and New York (1905). Cut off by the Russian Revolution, the 'Metropolia' became self-governing, received autocephaly from Moscow in 1970, and took its present name. Its autocephaly is not recognised by Constantinople and several other churches.
distinctives: Russian Alaskan mission and native Alaskan Orthodoxy
English-language liturgy and an American, multi-ethnic identity
St Vladimir's Seminary (Schmemann, Meyendorff) and St Tikhon's Seminary
Disputed autocephaly (1970)

traditions.name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
traditions.summary: Formed at a unification council in Kyiv's St Sophia Cathedral on 15 December 2018, chiefly from the Ukrainian Orthodox Church–Kyiv Patriarchate (1992) and the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church, and granted a Tomos of autocephaly by Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew in January 2019. Constantinople holds that Kyiv had always been its canonical territory and that it alone could heal the earlier schisms; Moscow holds that Ukraine is its canonical territory and broke communion with Constantinople. The Ukrainian Orthodox Church historically linked to Moscow continues alongside it.

Metropolitan Epiphanius (Dumenko) as primate
Recognised by Constantinople, Alexandria, Greece and Cyprus; not by Moscow and most others
Growing use of Ukrainian in the liturgy
Rapid parish transfers after Russia's 2022 invasion

traditions.name: Old Believers (Old Ritualists)
traditions.summary: Russian Orthodox Christians who refused Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms and the Great Moscow Council of 1666–67 that anathematised the old rites. Persecuted for centuries — Archpriest Avvakum was burned in 1682 — they divided into 'priestly' groups (popovtsy), which later obtained the Belokrinitsa hierarchy (1846), and 'priestless' groups (bezpopovtsy), which concluded that a valid priesthood had ceased. The Moscow Patriarchate lifted the anathemas on the old rites in 1971.
distinctives: Two-finger sign of the cross and pre-Nikonian service books
Strict preservation of ritual, icons and znamenny chant
Priestly and priestless branches
Communities in Siberia, the Baltic, Romania (Lipovans), Alaska, Oregon, Brazil and Bolivia

profile.canon: Old Testament from the Septuagint, including the books Protestants call deuterocanonical (anagignoskomena), and the 27-book New Testament.

traditions.summary: The church of the Russian emigration after the Civil War, organised in 1920–21 and headquartered successively in Sremski Karlovci, Munich and New York. It refused the 1927 declaration of loyalty to the Soviet state by Metropolitan Sergius, canonised the New Martyrs (1981) and was a voice of strict traditionalism. In 2007 it entered canonical communion with the Moscow Patriarchate as a self-governing church.

Western Rite parishes and English-language missions

profile.salvation: Salvation is theosis: union with God by grace through Christ in the Holy Spirit, received in baptism and lived out in faith, repentance, prayer and the sacramental life of the Church.

profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return, the resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed and the communion of saints; no doctrine of purgatory.
profile.governance: First Hierarch and Synod of Bishops in New York; self-governing within the Moscow Patriarchate since 2007.
profile.worship: Byzantine rite in Church Slavonic and local languages; Julian calendar.
profile.canon: Old Testament from the Septuagint, including the books Protestants call deuterocanonical (anagignoskomena), and the 27-book New Testament.

traditions.status: Active, self-governing part of the Moscow Patriarchate; a small minority rejected the 2007 union.

traditions.name: Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church
traditions.summary: After Eritrea's independence (1993), the Eritrean dioceses of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church obtained autocephaly through the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate; the first patriarch, Abune Philipos, was consecrated in 1998. It shares the Ge'ez liturgy, broad biblical canon and Miaphysite (often called Monophysite by opponents) Christology of the Ethiopian church. Patriarch Abune Antonios was removed in 2006 amid government involvement and held under house arrest until his death in 2022, a deposition many Orthodox bodies regarded as uncanonical.
distinctives: Ge'ez liturgy and the Tewahedo ('made one') Christology
Monastic centres such as Debre Bizen
Close state oversight of religion in Eritrea
Contested deposition of Patriarch Antonios (2006)

profile.authority: Scripture and the tradition of the first three ecumenical councils, the Fathers (especially Cyril of Alexandria) and the Ge'ez liturgical books.
profile.salvation: Salvation by the grace of the incarnate Word, received through faith, the sacraments, fasting and the life of the church.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; the Eucharist (Qurban) in the tabot-centred liturgy; circumcision and Old Testament food laws kept as custom.
profile.eschatology: Resurrection, judgement and prayer for the dead; strong devotion to Mary and the saints.
profile.governance: Patriarch and Holy Synod; strong state influence since 2006.
profile.worship: Ge'ez and Tigrinya liturgy, drums and sistra, extensive fasting (over 180 days a year for the devout).
profile.canon: Broad Ethiopian-tradition canon including Enoch and Jubilees.

traditions.status: Active; the church of a large share of Eritrea's Christians. Membership statistics are not reliably available.

traditions.name: Jacobite Syrian Christian Church (Malankara Syriac Orthodox)
traditions.summary: The part of the St Thomas Christians of Kerala that remains an integral, self-governing part of the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch under its Catholicos of India. It separated from the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church in the disputes that began in 1912, reunited in 1958 and divided again from 1975. A 2017 Supreme Court of India judgement in favour of the Malankara Orthodox claim on parishes led to transfers of disputed churches.
distinctives: Loyalty to the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch
West Syriac liturgy (Qurbono) in Malayalam and Syriac
'Jacobite' name from Jacob Baradaeus (6th century)
Long legal dispute with the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church

profile.authority: Scripture and the tradition of the Syriac Fathers and the first three ecumenical councils, with the Patriarch of Antioch as supreme head.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ received in faith, sacramental life, prayer and fasting.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments in the West Syriac rite; Holy Qurbono with the Liturgy of St James.
profile.eschatology: Resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed and intercession of the saints, especially Mary.
profile.governance: Catholicos of India (Maphrian) under the Patriarch of Antioch, with a local synod and the Malankara Jacobite Syrian Christian Association.
profile.worship: West Syriac liturgy in Malayalam and Syriac, with seven daily prayer hours.
profile.canon: Peshitta-tradition canon; in practice the broader Orthodox canon.

traditions.status: Active in Kerala and the diaspora; Catholicos Baselios Thomas I led it from 2002 until his death in 2024.

traditions.name: Mar Thoma Syrian Church of Malabar
traditions.summary: A 'reformed Oriental' church of Kerala that keeps the West Syriac liturgical structure and episcopal order of the St Thomas Christians while adopting Reformation emphases: vernacular worship, Scripture's sole authority in doctrine, and the removal of prayers for the dead and invocation of saints. It grew from the reforms of Abraham Malpan (1836) and separated after an 1889 court verdict. Its Maramon Convention is one of the largest Christian gatherings in Asia.
distinctives: Reformed West Syriac liturgy in Malayalam
Strong evangelistic and mission societies (Mar Thoma Evangelistic Association, 1888)
Communion relations with Anglican churches and the Church of South India
Maramon Convention (from 1895)
Member of the World Council of Churches

profile.authority: Holy Scripture as the supreme authority for faith, with the Nicene Creed and the Syriac liturgical heritage purified in its light.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, expressed in personal conversion, holiness and witness.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Holy Qurbana as the chief sacraments, celebrated in a revised Syriac rite; confirmation, marriage and ordination retained as rites.
profile.eschatology: Hope of Christ's return and eternal life; no prayers for the dead.
profile.governance: Metropolitan and episcopal synod with an elected representative assembly (Prathinidhi Mandalam) of clergy and laity.
profile.worship: Revised Liturgy of St James in Malayalam and other languages, with Bible study and evangelistic conventions.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active, with roughly a million members in India and the diaspora (church estimate).

traditions.name: Armenian Catholicosate of the Great House of Cilicia
traditions.summary: One of the two catholicosates of the Armenian Apostolic Church. The supreme see had followed the Armenian kingdom to Cilicia; when a new catholicos was elected at Etchmiadzin in 1441, the line at Sis continued. After the genocide and the loss of Cilicia it was re-established at Antelias near Beirut (1930). During the Cold War it led much of the diaspora independently of Soviet-controlled Etchmiadzin; it shares the same faith and liturgy and recognises Etchmiadzin's primacy of honour.
distinctives: Seat at Antelias, Lebanon
Jurisdiction over Lebanon, Syria, Cyprus, Iran, the Gulf and part of the North American diaspora
Cold War-era rivalry and later cooperation with Etchmiadzin
Active ecumenical role in the Middle East Council of Churches and WCC

profile.authority: Scripture and the tradition of the first three ecumenical councils, the Armenian Fathers (e.g. Gregory the Illuminator, Nerses Shnorhali) and the Armenian liturgy.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through the incarnate Christ, received in faith and the sacramental life.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; unleavened bread and unmixed wine in the Eucharist (Badarak); infant communion.
profile.eschatology: Resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed; veneration of saints, including the genocide martyrs canonised in 2015.
profile.governance: Catholicos (Aram I since 1995) elected by a national ecclesiastical assembly of clergy and laity.
profile.worship: Armenian Divine Liturgy in Classical Armenian; Christmas and Theophany kept together on 6 January.
profile.canon: The Armenian Bible, broadly the Orthodox canon.

traditions.status: Active; leads several diaspora dioceses alongside Etchmiadzin's.

traditions.name: Ancient Church of the East
traditions.summary: A branch of the Church of the East that separated from the Assyrian Church of the East in 1968, when opponents of Patriarch Eshai Shimun XXIII's adoption of the Gregorian calendar and of hereditary patriarchal succession consecrated Mar Thoma Darmo as patriarch in Baghdad. It shares the East Syriac faith, liturgy and heritage of the Assyrian church; dialogue on reunion has continued for decades.
distinctives: Retention of the Julian calendar
Patriarchate in Baghdad
Rejection of hereditary patriarchal succession (later also ended in the Assyrian church)
Reunion talks with the Assyrian Church of the East

profile.authority: Scripture and the East Syriac Fathers (Theodore of Mopsuestia, Narsai, Babai the Great) and the synods of the Church of the East.
profile.salvation: Salvation through Christ, the eternal Word who took a complete humanity, received through faith, baptism and the Holy Qurbana.
profile.sacraments: Sacraments ('Raze') including baptism, Eucharist, ordination and the Holy Leaven; the Anaphora of Addai and Mari.
profile.eschatology: Resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed.
profile.governance: Catholicos-Patriarch (Mar Addai II, 1972–2022, then his successor) with a synod of metropolitans and bishops.
profile.worship: East Syriac liturgy in Syriac with Neo-Aramaic; Julian calendar.
profile.canon: Peshitta canon (traditionally 22 New Testament books).

traditions.status: Active, small, concentrated in Iraq and the diaspora.

traditions.name: Chaldean Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The East Syriac church in communion with Rome, originating in the 1552–53 election and papal consecration of Yohannan Sulaqa and consolidated as a single 'Patriarchate of Babylon of the Chaldeans' in 1830. It is the largest church of Iraq; its patriarchate moved from Mosul to Baghdad in 1950. War, the 2014 Islamic State expulsions from Mosul and the Nineveh Plains, and emigration have greatly reduced its Iraqi presence and enlarged its diaspora (notably Detroit and San Diego).
distinctives: East Syriac liturgy in communion with Rome
Largest Christian community in Iraq
Seat in Baghdad; Cardinal Louis Raphaël I Sako patriarch from 2013
Large diaspora in the United States, Australia and Europe

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition with the magisterium of the Pope and bishops; the East Syriac Fathers and liturgy.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments, as in Catholic teaching.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments in the East Syriac (Chaldean) rite; the Anaphora of Addai and Mari.
profile.eschatology: Catholic eschatology: resurrection, judgement, heaven, purgatory and hell.
profile.governance: Patriarch and synod as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990).
profile.worship: Chaldean liturgy in Syriac, Neo-Aramaic, Arabic and English.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon.

traditions.status: Active; c. 630,000 faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Maronite Church
traditions.summary: A Syriac-heritage church named after the hermit St Maron (d. c. 410) and the monastery founded in his memory; tradition names John Maron (d. 707) as its first patriarch. Maronites hold that they have never been out of communion with Rome; formal ties were reaffirmed during the Crusades (1182) and the Synod of Mount Lebanon (1736) codified their discipline. Centred on Mount Lebanon, the church has shaped modern Lebanon and has a large emigrant community, especially in Brazil and the Americas.
distinctives: The only Eastern Catholic church with no Orthodox counterpart
West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy in Syriac and Arabic
Patriarchal seat at Bkerké, Lebanon
Monastic and hermit tradition of the Qadisha valley
Large global diaspora

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; Maronite Qurbono with Syriac anaphoras; historic latinisations partly reversed since Vatican II.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Patriarch of Antioch and All the East (Bechara Boutros al-Rahi since 2011) with the synod of bishops, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Maronite liturgy in Arabic and Syriac (and local languages abroad); Syriac chant.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 3.5 million faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Melkite Greek Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The Byzantine-rite Arabic-speaking church in communion with Rome, formed when the 1724 patriarchal election in Antioch divided pro-Roman and pro-Constantinople parties. 'Melkite' (from Syriac malka, 'king') originally named the Chalcedonian 'imperial' Christians. At Vatican II, Patriarch Maximos IV Sayegh became a prominent defender of Eastern traditions and the dignity of the Eastern churches.
distinctives: Byzantine liturgy in Arabic and Greek
Patriarch of Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem, resident in Damascus
Advocacy of Eastern ecclesiology within Catholicism (Maximos IV at Vatican II)
Close cultural kinship with the Antiochian Orthodox

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven Mysteries in the Byzantine rite; chrismation and communion given to infants at baptism.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Patriarch (Youssef Absi since 2017) with the Holy Synod, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom in Arabic, Greek and English; Byzantine chant.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 1.6 million faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The largest Eastern Catholic church, born of the Union of Brest (1596), by which bishops of the Kyivan metropolia accepted papal authority while keeping their Byzantine rite. Suppressed in the Russian Empire, it flourished in Habsburg Galicia, especially under Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky (1901–44). The Soviet-staged 'Synod of Lviv' (1946) abolished it, and it survived underground until 1989. Its Major Archbishop has resided in Kyiv since 2005.
distinctives: Byzantine rite with married clergy
Martyrdom and underground existence under Soviet rule (1946–1989)
Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky and the rescue of Jews during the Holocaust
Strong role in Ukrainian national and civic life
Seat in Kyiv; Major Archbishop Sviatoslav Shevchuk since 2011

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven Mysteries in the Byzantine rite; infant communion restored in many eparchies.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Major Archbishop of Kyiv-Halych with the Synod of Bishops, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Divine Liturgy in Ukrainian and Church Slavonic; Julian calendar historically, with a move to the Revised Julian calendar in 2023.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 4.5 million faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Syro-Malabar Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The majority of the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, who trace their faith to the apostle Thomas and inherited the East Syriac liturgy from the Church of the East. Latinised under Portuguese rule after the Synod of Diamper (1599), the community split after the Coonan Cross Oath (1653); those who stayed with Rome became the Syro-Malabar Church. It received its own Indian hierarchy in 1923 and major archiepiscopal status in 1992, and is notable for numerous priestly and religious vocations serving worldwide.
distinctives: East Syriac liturgical heritage of the St Thomas Christians
Very high number of priests and religious
Major Archbishop in Ernakulam (Raphael Thattil since 2024)
Internal dispute since the 1990s over how the Qurbana is celebrated (facing the people or the altar)

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; the Holy Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition (Anaphora of Addai and Mari), with retained Latin influences.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Major Archbishop of Ernakulam-Angamaly with the Synod of Bishops, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Holy Qurbana in Malayalam and Syriac; distinctive St Thomas Christian customs (e.g. the 'Mar Thoma Sleeva' cross).
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 4.25 million faithful (2017), the second-largest Eastern Catholic church.

traditions.name: Syro-Malankara Catholic Church
traditions.summary: A church of Kerala formed when Archbishop Geevarghese Mar Ivanios, founder of the Bethany monastic order, and Bishop Jacob Mar Theophilos of the Malankara Orthodox Church entered Catholic communion in 1930, keeping the West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy. It became a major archiepiscopal church in 2005.
distinctives: Antiochene (West Syriac) rite in communion with Rome
Reunion movement led by Mar Ivanios (1930)
Bethany monastic congregations
Seat at Thiruvananthapuram; Major Archbishop Baselios Cleemis since 2007

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; Holy Qurbono of St James in the West Syriac rite.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Major Archbishop-Catholicos of Trivandrum with the Holy Episcopal Synod, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: West Syriac liturgy in Malayalam and Syriac.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 470,000 faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Coptic Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The Alexandrian-rite church in communion with Rome. Its organised history begins in 1741, when the Coptic bishop Amba Athanasius of Jerusalem became Catholic and Rome created a vicariate for Catholic Copts; the patriarchate was effectively established by Leo XIII in 1895. It runs a substantial network of schools and social services in Upper Egypt.
distinctives: Coptic (Alexandrian) liturgy in Coptic and Arabic
Patriarch of Alexandria resident in Cairo
Schools and social work especially in Upper Egypt
Minority beside the much larger Coptic Orthodox Church

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments in the Coptic rite (anaphoras of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril).
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Patriarch of Alexandria (Ibrahim Isaac Sidrak since 2013) with the synod, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Coptic liturgy in Coptic and Arabic with Coptic chant and percussion.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 190,000 faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Ethiopian and Eritrean Catholic Churches (Ge'ez rite)
traditions.summary: The Ge'ez-rite Catholic churches of Ethiopia and Eritrea. After the failed Jesuit-led union of the 17th century, a lasting Catholic community grew from the mission of St Justin de Jacobis (from 1839). An ordinariate for Ge'ez-rite Catholics was created in 1930, a metropolitan church sui iuris in Addis Ababa in 1961, and a separate Eritrean Catholic Church sui iuris in 2015.
distinctives: Ge'ez (Alexandrian-Ethiopian) liturgy in communion with Rome
Legacy of St Justin de Jacobis and indigenous clergy
Two churches sui iuris since 2015 (Addis Ababa and Asmara)
Schools, clinics and development work

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments in the Ge'ez rite.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Metropolitan archbishops of Addis Ababa and Asmara, each with a council of hierarchs, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Ge'ez liturgy with Amharic, Tigrinya and other languages; Ethiopian chant and calendar.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; small minorities in both countries.

traditions.name: Armenian Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The Armenian-rite church in communion with Rome, constituted when Pope Benedict XIV confirmed Abraham Petros I Ardzivian as Patriarch of Cilicia of the Armenians in 1742. The Mekhitarist monks of San Lazzaro in Venice (from 1717) made it a centre of Armenian scholarship. Devastated by the 1915 genocide, the patriarchate has resided in Beirut since 1928.
distinctives: Armenian liturgy in communion with Rome
Mekhitarist Order (Venice and Vienna) and Armenian learning
Martyrdom in 1915 (e.g. Bishop Ignatius Maloyan, beatified 2001 and canonised 2025)
Patriarchate at Bzommar and Beirut, Lebanon

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments in the Armenian rite; unleavened bread in the Eucharist.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Patriarch-Catholicos of Cilicia of the Armenian Catholics with the synod, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: Armenian Divine Liturgy in Classical Armenian.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 750,000 faithful reported (2017).

traditions.name: Syriac Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The West Syriac church in communion with Rome. A Catholic patriarch, Andrew Akhijan, was installed in Aleppo in 1662, but the line lapsed in 1702; it was renewed in 1782–83 by Michael Jarweh, who had been elected Syriac Orthodox patriarch and declared himself Catholic, establishing the patriarchal monastery of Sharfeh in Lebanon. Its patriarch resides in Beirut; its Iraqi communities (Qaraqosh/Bakhdida) suffered displacement by the Islamic State in 2014.
distinctives: West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy in communion with Rome
Sharfeh monastery, Lebanon
Strongholds in the Nineveh Plains, Syria and Lebanon
Patriarch Ignatius Joseph III Younan since 2009

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; Syriac liturgy of St James.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
profile.governance: Patriarch of Antioch of the Syriacs with the synod, governed as a church sui iuris under the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (1990), in full communion with the Bishop of Rome.
profile.worship: West Syriac liturgy in Syriac and Arabic with Syriac chant.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; displaced communities in Iraq and Syria and a growing diaspora.

traditions.name: Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church
traditions.summary: The Byzantine-rite Catholic church of the Carpatho-Rusyn people, founded at the Union of Uzhhorod (1646). Its Mukachevo eparchy in Transcarpathia was liquidated by the Soviets in 1949 and restored in 1989. Immigrants brought it to the United States, where disputes with Latin bishops over married priests led many to join Orthodoxy (from 1891), while the remainder became the Byzantine Catholic Metropolitan Church of Pittsburgh.
distinctives: Carpatho-Rusyn identity and prostopinije chant
Union of Uzhhorod (1646)
Soviet suppression (1949–1989)
American metropolitan church sui iuris (Pittsburgh)

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition interpreted by the magisterium of the Pope and bishops, together with the church's own patristic and liturgical heritage.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, received in faith and the sacraments; Eastern Catholics often express this, like the Orthodox, as deification (theosis).
profile.sacraments: Seven Mysteries in the Byzantine rite.
profile.eschatology: Catholic teaching on resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell, with prayer for the departed; Eastern Catholics often describe purification after death in Eastern rather than Latin terms.
