profile.worship: Byzantine liturgy in Church Slavonic, Rusyn and English with prostopinije ('plain chant').
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (73 books).

traditions.status: Active; c. 420,000 faithful (2017).

traditions.name: Polish National Catholic Church
traditions.summary: A church founded among Polish immigrants in Scranton, Pennsylvania, in 1897 under Fr (later Bishop) Francis Hodur, after disputes with the Roman Catholic hierarchy over parish property and Polish leadership. Hodur received episcopal consecration from Old Catholic bishops at Utrecht in 1907. The church belonged to the Union of Utrecht until 2003, when it withdrew over the ordination of women and related changes in other Old Catholic churches.
distinctives: Lay ownership and control of parish property
Vernacular (Polish, later English) Mass from the early twentieth century
Married clergy permitted
Proclamation of the Word of God, heard and preached, counted as a sacrament
Ongoing dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition as received in the undivided church of the first millennium; no recognition of papal infallibility or universal jurisdiction.
profile.salvation: Salvation by God's grace through Christ received in faith and the sacraments.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments, with the Word of God additionally treated as a sacrament; general (public) confession for adults alongside private confession.
profile.eschatology: Catholic hope of resurrection and eternal life; Hodur's teaching that all may ultimately reach salvation has been influential.
profile.governance: Bishops with a Prime Bishop and General Synods including clergy and laity.
profile.worship: Latin-rite Mass in English and Polish.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon.

traditions.status: Active; small, mainly in the north-eastern United States and Poland.

traditions.name: Independent Catholic movement
traditions.summary: A loose movement of small churches outside the Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican communions that claim apostolic succession through 'wandering bishops' (episcopi vagantes). Many lines derive from Arnold Harris Mathew, consecrated by Old Catholic bishops in 1908, from Joseph René Vilatte, consecrated by a Syriac Orthodox bishop in Ceylon in 1892, or from the Brazilian bishop Carlos Duarte Costa (1945). Theological positions range from traditionalist to very liberal.
distinctives: Claim of valid apostolic succession outside the large communions
Great diversity and frequent fragmentation
Often married, women or LGBTQ clergy in progressive jurisdictions
Sacramental Catholic worship in the vernacular
Not recognised by the Roman Catholic Church as being in communion

profile.authority: Varies by jurisdiction: typically Scripture, the creeds and Catholic tradition without papal jurisdiction.
profile.salvation: Generally Catholic sacramental understanding of salvation.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments, often with open communion.
profile.eschatology: Generally creedal; varies widely.
profile.governance: Small dioceses or jurisdictions led by bishops; many congregations meet in homes or borrowed churches.
profile.worship: Latin-rite (sometimes Tridentine, sometimes contemporary) liturgy in local languages.
profile.canon: Usually the Catholic canon.

traditions.status: Active as hundreds of small, often short-lived jurisdictions; reliable aggregate statistics do not exist.

traditions.name: Society of St Pius X (SSPX)
traditions.summary: A priestly society founded in 1970 at Fribourg by Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre with initial diocesan approval, whose seminary at Écône trained priests in the pre-conciliar liturgy. Approval was withdrawn in 1975, and Lefebvre's consecration of four bishops in 1988 without papal mandate was declared by Rome to incur excommunication. Benedict XVI lifted the bishops' excommunications in 2009 and Francis granted SSPX priests faculties for confession (2015), but the Holy See holds that the Society has no canonical status and its ministers do not legitimately exercise ministry. The Society regards itself as fully Catholic, acting from a state of necessity.
distinctives: Exclusive use of the 1962 Roman Missal (Traditional Latin Mass)
Critique of Vatican II teaching on religious liberty, ecumenism and collegiality
Irregular canonical status: neither formally in schism (per many Vatican statements) nor in full regular communion
Worldwide network of priories, schools and seminaries

profile.authority: Scripture and Tradition with the papacy and the pre-conciliar magisterium; the Society holds that some post-conciliar teaching departs from Tradition.
profile.salvation: Catholic doctrine of grace, merit and the sacraments as defined at Trent.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments in the pre-1970 rites.
profile.eschatology: Catholic eschatology (heaven, hell, purgatory, judgement).
profile.governance: Superior General and General Council; bishops without territorial jurisdiction.
profile.worship: Traditional Latin Mass and Divine Office with Gregorian chant.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon (Vulgate tradition).

traditions.status: Active, with several hundred priests worldwide; relations with Rome remain unresolved.

traditions.name: Philippine Independent Church (Iglesia Filipina Independiente)
traditions.summary: A nationalist church proclaimed in 1902 by Isabelo de los Reyes and led by its first Obispo Máximo, Gregorio Aglipay, in reaction to Spanish friar control of the Philippine church. Early leaders drifted towards Unitarian theology, but the 1947 Declaration of Faith and Articles of Religion restored Trinitarian orthodoxy; Episcopal Church bishops consecrated its bishops in 1948 and the two churches entered full communion in 1961. It is known for its commitment to social justice and Filipino identity.
distinctives: Filipino nationalist origins in the Revolution
Full communion with the Episcopal Church and wider Anglican Communion
Commitment to labour and social-justice causes (several clergy killed in recent decades)
Ordination of women (from 1997)
Catholic worship in Filipino languages

profile.authority: Scripture, the creeds and Catholic tradition as summarised in its Declaration of Faith (1947).
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ received in faith and the sacraments.
profile.sacraments: Seven sacraments; the Filipino Missal.
profile.eschatology: Creedal hope of Christ's return and eternal life.
profile.governance: Supreme Bishop (Obispo Máximo) with a General Assembly and Supreme Council of Bishops.
profile.worship: Vernacular Catholic liturgy in Filipino and other Philippine languages.
profile.canon: The Catholic canon.

traditions.status: Active; one of the largest non-Roman churches in the Philippines.

traditions.name: Church of Sweden
traditions.summary: Sweden's national Lutheran church, which grew from Gustav Vasa's break with Rome at the Riksdag of Västerås (1527) and the preaching of Olaus and Laurentius Petri, and confirmed its confessional Lutheranism at the Uppsala Synod (1593). It kept a historic episcopate. A state church until 2000, it was among the first to ordain women (1960) and to approve church weddings for same-sex couples (2009).
distinctives: Historic episcopal succession claimed through the Reformation
Archbishop of Uppsala as primate
Member of the Porvoo Communion with British and Irish Anglicans
Theologically liberal, socially prominent folk church (folkkyrka)
Disestablished in 2000

profile.authority: Scripture as the norming norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions of the Book of Concord as a faithful exposition (norma normata).
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
profile.eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
profile.governance: Episcopal and synodical: bishops with a General Synod (Kyrkomötet) whose members are elected in church elections organised partly by political nominating groups.
profile.worship: Swedish High Mass (Högmässa), rich hymnody and choral tradition.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; membership has declined steadily but remains just over half of Sweden's population.

traditions.name: Church of Norway
traditions.summary: Norway's Lutheran church, imposed by the Danish crown through the Church Ordinance of 1537 (applied in Norway 1539). Lay revival movements, especially the Haugean awakening led by Hans Nielsen Hauge (from 1796), shaped its popular piety and mission societies. Its formal state-church status ended with constitutional changes in 2012 and its separation as an independent legal entity in 2017.
distinctives: Folk church with high membership
Strong lay revival and mission organisations (Haugean heritage)
Bishops and a General Synod; separated from the state 2012–2017
Approved church weddings for same-sex couples (2016)

profile.authority: Scripture as the norming norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions of the Book of Concord as a faithful exposition (norma normata).
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
profile.eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
profile.governance: Bishops' Conference, diocesan councils and a General Synod (Kirkemøtet) with lay majorities.
profile.worship: Norwegian Lutheran liturgy (revised 2011), hymnody in Bokmål, Nynorsk and Sami.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; membership has declined but includes a majority of Norwegians.

traditions.name: Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD) and the union churches
traditions.summary: The federation of twenty regional Protestant churches (Landeskirchen) of Germany — Lutheran, Reformed and United. Union churches began with the Prussian Union of 1817, when Friedrich Wilhelm III united Lutheran and Reformed congregations. The EKD was founded at Treysa in 1945 after the Church Struggle under Nazism, in which the Confessing Church's Barmen Declaration (1934) challenged the pro-Nazi 'German Christians'. The Leuenberg Agreement (1973) established pulpit and table fellowship among its traditions.
distinctives: Federation of Lutheran, Reformed and United regional churches
Prussian Union (1817) and its Old Lutheran critics
Legacy of the Church Struggle and the Barmen Declaration
Church tax collected by the state
Leuenberg Agreement (1973) on Lutheran–Reformed fellowship

profile.authority: Scripture, with each regional church bound to its own confessions (Lutheran, Reformed or both); the Barmen Declaration widely received.
profile.salvation: Justification by grace through faith, as affirmed in the Reformation confessions and the Joint Declaration of 1999 (on the Lutheran side).
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper, with mutual recognition between Lutheran and Reformed understandings under Leuenberg.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return and the resurrection; modern theology has often reinterpreted traditional eschatology.
profile.governance: Federal: regional synods and bishops or church presidents; an EKD Synod, Council and Church Conference.
profile.worship: Lutheran and Reformed liturgies (Agende), strong choral and organ traditions.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; membership has fallen steeply but remains around one fifth of Germany's population.

traditions.name: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod
traditions.summary: A confessional Lutheran church founded in Chicago in 1847 by German immigrants, notably Saxon Lutherans led by C. F. W. Walther, who had emigrated in 1838–39 partly to escape rationalism and the Prussian-style union. It subscribes unconditionally ('because', quia) to the Book of Concord, teaches biblical inerrancy, practises closed communion and does not ordain women. A 1970s conflict over biblical interpretation led to the 'Seminex' walkout (1974) from Concordia Seminary.
distinctives: Quia subscription to the entire Book of Concord
Biblical inerrancy
Closed (close) communion
Pastoral office reserved to men
Extensive parochial school system and Concordia universities

profile.authority: Scripture as the inerrant Word of God; the Lutheran Confessions accepted because they agree with Scripture.
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
profile.eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
profile.governance: Congregational-synodical polity with a synod president and districts; congregations call their pastors.
profile.worship: Liturgical worship from the Lutheran Service Book (2006), alongside contemporary services.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; c. 1.8 million baptised members in the early 2020s, slowly declining.

traditions.name: Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA)
traditions.summary: The largest Lutheran church in the United States, formed in 1987–88 from the American Lutheran Church, the Lutheran Church in America and the Association of Evangelical Lutheran Churches. It ordains women (as its predecessors had since 1970), has full-communion agreements with Reformed churches (1997), the Episcopal Church (1999), the Moravians and the United Methodists, and in 2009 permitted pastors in committed same-sex relationships, after which some congregations formed the NALC and LCMC.
distinctives: Ecumenical full-communion agreements
Ordination of women and LGBTQ clergy
Historic episcopate adopted through 'Called to Common Mission' (1999)
Strong social-ministry organisations

profile.authority: Scripture as the norming norm (norma normans), with the Lutheran Confessions of the Book of Concord as a faithful exposition (norma normata).
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper, in which Christ's true body and blood are present 'in, with and under' the bread and wine; private confession and absolution retained.
profile.eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
profile.governance: Presiding bishop, churchwide assembly and 65 synods each led by a bishop.
profile.worship: Liturgical worship from Evangelical Lutheran Worship (2006).
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; c. 2.8 million baptised members in the early 2020s, declining.

traditions.name: Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus
traditions.summary: An Ethiopian Lutheran church formed in 1959 from congregations founded by Scandinavian, German and American missions together with indigenous evangelical movements; Presbyterian-origin synods joined in 1974. Persecuted under the Marxist Derg — its general secretary Gudina Tumsa was murdered in 1979 — it grew rapidly to become one of the largest Lutheran churches in the world. It combines Lutheran confession with a strong charismatic and evangelistic piety.
distinctives: Holistic ministry: 'serving the whole person' (evangelism and development)
Charismatic renewal within a Lutheran confession
Martyrdom of Gudina Tumsa (1979)
Broke fellowship with the Church of Sweden and the ELCA in 2013 over same-sex marriage
Mekane Yesus Seminary in Addis Ababa

profile.authority: Scripture as the Word of God, with the ecumenical creeds, the Augsburg Confession and Luther's Small Catechism.
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper with Lutheran real-presence teaching; healing prayer and deliverance commonly practised.
profile.eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
profile.governance: President and General Assembly with regional synods; Lutheran and Presbyterian elements combined.
profile.worship: Lively worship in Amharic, Oromo and other languages with indigenous music and prayer for healing.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active and growing; reported by the Lutheran World Federation as having over ten million members.

traditions.name: Batak Christian Protestant Church (HKBP)
traditions.summary: The Huria Kristen Batak Protestan, the largest Protestant church in Indonesia, born of the Rhenish Mission among the Toba Batak of North Sumatra, especially through Ludwig Ingwer Nommensen (from 1862). It became autonomous in 1930, received its first Batak ephorus in 1940, and in 1951 adopted its own Confession of Faith — an early example of an Asian church writing its own confession — which allowed it to join the Lutheran World Federation (1952) while retaining a United (Lutheran-Reformed) heritage.
distinctives: Rhenish (United) mission heritage with Lutheran confessional identity
HKBP Confession (1951), addressing local questions such as ancestral practices
Ephorus as head of the church
Strong Batak ethnic and cultural identity
Batak church music and choirs

profile.authority: Scripture, the ecumenical creeds and the HKBP Confession of Faith (1951, revised 1996).
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and Holy Communion; confirmation of youth.
profile.eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
profile.governance: Ephorus with a synod (Synode Godang) and districts (distrik); church order of 1930 and later revisions.
profile.worship: Liturgical worship in Batak and Indonesian with large choirs and hymnody (Buku Ende).
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; several million members in Indonesia and the Batak diaspora.

traditions.name: Laestadianism (Laestadian Lutheran revival)
traditions.summary: A conservative Lutheran revival movement begun by Lars Levi Laestadius, pastor in Swedish Lapland, after his awakening in 1844. It spread among Sami, Finns, Swedes and Norwegians and, through emigration, to North America. In the Nordic countries it remains mostly within the national Lutheran churches as lay associations; in North America it formed separate churches (e.g. the Laestadian Lutheran Church and Apostolic Lutheran churches). It has divided into several branches.
distinctives: Forgiveness of sins proclaimed by one believer to another 'in Jesus' name and blood'
Strong sense of the believing congregation as the true church
Conservative lifestyle (e.g. large families, avoidance of contraception in some branches)
Summer services (suviseurat) drawing tens of thousands
Origins among the Sami and in the far north

profile.authority: Scripture and the Lutheran Confessions, with the living word of the believing congregation as the bearer of forgiveness.
profile.salvation: Justification by faith, experienced through hearing and believing the absolution spoken by a fellow believer.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper (often received in the national church), with spoken absolution central.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return and eternal life; strong emphasis on remaining in living faith until the end.
profile.governance: Lay preachers and associations within the national churches; separate congregational churches in North America.
profile.worship: Simple preaching services led by lay preachers, Zion's hymns and the songs of the revival.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active in northern Finland, Sweden, Norway and the United States; several branches with differing relations to each other.

traditions.name: Church of Scotland
traditions.summary: Scotland's national Presbyterian church, shaped by the Reformation Parliament of 1560, John Knox and the Scots Confession, and Andrew Melville's Presbyterian polity. After a century of struggle with episcopacy, Presbyterian government was settled in 1690. The Disruption of 1843, over patronage and spiritual independence, split it nearly in half; most of the separated bodies reunited with it in 1929. It is a national church recognised by the state but not controlled by it (Church of Scotland Act 1921).
distinctives: Presbyterian government by kirk sessions, presbyteries and the General Assembly
Westminster Confession as subordinate standard
Spiritual independence from the state (1921 Act)
Ordination of women ministers since 1968
Iona Community (founded 1938) and Scottish psalmody

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The Westminster Confession is its principal subordinate standard, with liberty of opinion on points not entering the substance of the faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: elders and ministers in courts of kirk session, presbytery and General Assembly, with an annually chosen Moderator.
profile.worship: Reformed worship centred on preaching; metrical psalms, the Church Hymnary; Communion seasons historically infrequent.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active; membership has fallen sharply to under 300,000 by the 2020s.

traditions.name: Dutch Reformed Church (NHK) and Protestant Church in the Netherlands (PKN)
traditions.summary: The Reformed public church of the Netherlands, organised by the exiles' Synod of Emden (1571) and confirmed in its Calvinist orthodoxy by the Synod of Dort (1618–19). Reorganised in 1816 as the Nederlandse Hervormde Kerk, it suffered secessions in 1834 (Afscheiding) and 1886 (Doleantie, led by Abraham Kuyper), which produced the Gereformeerde Kerken. In 2004 the Hervormde Kerk, the Gereformeerde Kerken and the Evangelical-Lutheran Church merged as the Protestant Church in the Netherlands (PKN); dissenting congregations formed the Restored Reformed Church.
distinctives: Three Forms of Unity (Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Canons of Dort)
Secessions of 1834 and 1886 and the 2004 merger
Neo-Calvinism of Abraham Kuyper (in the Gereformeerde line)
Mother church of Reformed churches in South Africa, Indonesia and North America

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The PKN's church order also includes the Lutheran confessions and the Barmen Declaration.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian-synodal: consistories, classes and a General Synod.
profile.worship: Reformed worship with Genevan psalms and the Liedboek; a strong orthodox 'Bible Belt' wing alongside liberal congregations.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active as the PKN, the largest Protestant church in the Netherlands, though declining.

traditions.name: Reformed Church in Hungary
traditions.summary: The Calvinist church of Hungarian speakers, consolidated when the Synod of Debrecen (1567) adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism. It flourished in Transylvania and eastern Hungary under Ottoman and Transylvanian rule, survived Habsburg Counter-Reformation pressure, and today also has sister churches among Hungarian minorities in Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine and Serbia.
distinctives: Second Helvetic Confession and Heidelberg Catechism
Debrecen as 'the Calvinist Rome'
Historic colleges at Debrecen and Sárospatak
Strong link between Reformed faith and Hungarian identity
Bishops within a Presbyterian-synodal order

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards).
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian-synodal with bishops presiding over church districts alongside lay chief curators.
profile.worship: Reformed worship with Genevan psalms in Hungarian and preaching; churches without images.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active; the second-largest church in Hungary.

traditions.name: Christian Reformed Church in North America
traditions.summary: A church of Dutch immigrant origin founded in west Michigan in 1857 by congregations that left the Reformed Protestant Dutch Church (today's Reformed Church in America). Shaped by the Seceder tradition and by Abraham Kuyper's neo-Calvinism, it built Calvin University and Seminary and a strong Christian school movement. It opened all offices to women in 1995 (by local option); in 2022 its synod declared that its confessions exclude same-sex sexual relationships, leading some congregations to leave.
distinctives: Three Forms of Unity
Kuyperian vision of Christ's lordship over all of life
Christian day schools and Calvin University
Dutch-Canadian and Dutch-American heritage now becoming multi-ethnic

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Officers subscribe to the Three Forms of Unity.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: councils, classes and an annual synod.
profile.worship: Reformed worship with psalms and hymns (Psalter Hymnal; Lift Up Your Hearts).
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active in the United States and Canada; roughly 200,000 members.

traditions.name: Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)
traditions.summary: The largest Presbyterian church in the United States, formed in 1983 by the reunion of the northern UPCUSA and southern PCUS, divided since 1861. It traces its roots to the first American presbytery (Philadelphia, 1706). Its Book of Confessions includes historic creeds, the Westminster Standards, the Barmen Declaration, the Confession of 1967 and the Confession of Belhar. It ordains women and, since 2011 and 2014 decisions, LGBTQ clergy and same-sex marriages, changes that led many congregations to depart.
distinctives: Book of Confessions spanning the early church to the twentieth century
Ecumenical commitments (full communion with the ELCA, 1997)
Ordination of women and LGBTQ people
Substantial departures to the PCA, EPC and ECO since the 2000s

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The Book of Confessions as a collection of subordinate standards.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries, synods and a biennial General Assembly with co-moderators.
profile.worship: Reformed liturgy (Book of Common Worship), hymnal Glory to God (2013).
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active; c. 1.1 million members (2023), declining.

traditions.name: Presbyterian Church in America (PCA)
traditions.summary: A conservative Presbyterian church formed in 1973 by congregations leaving the southern PCUS, describing itself as 'faithful to the Scriptures, true to the Reformed faith, and obedient to the Great Commission'. In 1982 it received the Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod. It holds to biblical inerrancy and the Westminster Standards, ordains only men as elders and ministers, and has grown through church planting in cities.
distinctives: Westminster Confession and Catechisms
Biblical inerrancy
Ordination of men only to church office
Urban church planting (e.g. Redeemer Presbyterian, New York)
Strong ties with Reformed seminaries

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Officers subscribe to the Westminster Standards.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and an annual General Assembly.
profile.worship: Reformed worship ranging from traditional to contemporary.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active; c. 390,000 members, growing slowly.

traditions.name: Presbyterian Church of Korea (Tonghap and Hapdong)
traditions.summary: Korean Presbyterianism grew from American, Australian and Canadian missions using the 'Nevius method' of self-support. Its first independent presbytery was organised in 1907, the year of the Pyongyang Great Revival. After the colonial-era Shinto shrine controversy and post-war divisions, the 1959 General Assembly split into the ecumenical Tonghap (PCK) and the more conservative Hapdong (GAPCK), each today among the largest Presbyterian denominations in the world.
distinctives: Dawn prayer meetings and fervent evangelism
Legacy of the Shinto shrine controversy (1938)
Tonghap a member of the WCC; Hapdong outside it
Large congregations and global missionary sending
Many further splits (Kosin, Kijang, and others)

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Both main bodies hold the Westminster Standards; Hapdong stresses inerrancy more strongly.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and a General Assembly for each denomination.
profile.worship: Preaching-centred worship with early-morning and overnight prayer, tongsong kido (praying aloud together).
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active; each main body reports over two million members, though numbers have fallen since the 2010s.

traditions.name: French Reformed Church (Huguenots)
traditions.summary: The Reformed churches of France, organised at a secret national synod in Paris in 1559 with the Gallican Confession. Their members, called Huguenots, endured the Wars of Religion and the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572), gained toleration by the Edict of Nantes (1598), and lost it with its revocation (1685), which drove some 200,000 into exile in Europe, South Africa and North America. Those who stayed formed the 'Church of the Desert'. In 2013 the Reformed Church of France united with the Lutherans as the United Protestant Church of France.
distinctives: Gallican (La Rochelle) Confession
Experience of persecution, exile (the Refuge) and the 'Desert'
Camisard uprising (1702–1704) in the Cévennes
Protestant contribution to French secularism (laïcité)
United Protestant Church of France (2013)

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The La Rochelle Confession holds historic honour.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Presbyterian-synodal: consistories (presbyteral councils), regional synods and a national synod.
profile.worship: Sober Reformed worship centred on preaching and Psalms (Genevan Psalter).
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active as part of the United Protestant Church of France and other Reformed bodies.

traditions.name: Swiss Reformed Churches
traditions.summary: The cantonal Reformed churches of Switzerland, rooted in Zwingli's Zurich Reformation (from 1523), Bullinger's leadership, Bern's reform (1528) and Calvin's Geneva. The Consensus Tigurinus (1549) united Zurich and Geneva on the Lord's Supper and the Second Helvetic Confession (1566) became an international Reformed standard. Each canton's church is self-governing; since the nineteenth century most have not bound members to a confession. They federated in 1920 and became the Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland in 2020.
distinctives: Zurich and Geneva as twin cradles of the Reformed tradition
Second Helvetic Confession (1566)
Cantonal (Landeskirche) structure, often publicly recognised
Historic freedom from binding confessions since the 19th century
Prophesying (Prophezei) and biblical scholarship

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Most cantonal churches today treat confessions as historic witnesses rather than binding standards.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
profile.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
profile.governance: Cantonal synods and church councils; national Evangelical Reformed Church of Switzerland (EKS) since 2020.
profile.worship: Simple, preaching-centred worship; Communion a few times a year in many congregations.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon.

traditions.status: Active; membership has declined to under a fifth of the Swiss population.

traditions.name: Church of England
traditions.summary: The established church of England and mother church of the Anglican Communion. Separated from Rome by Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534), given Protestant formularies under Edward VI and Elizabeth I (Book of Common Prayer, Thirty-Nine Articles), and shaped by the 1662 settlement, it holds together evangelical, Anglo-Catholic and liberal traditions. The monarch is Supreme Governor; bishops sit in the House of Lords. It ordained women priests from 1994 and bishops from 2014.
distinctives: Established church with the monarch as Supreme Governor
Book of Common Prayer (1662) and Thirty-Nine Articles
Parish system covering every part of England
Coexistence of evangelical, catholic and liberal traditions
Archbishop of Canterbury as focus of unity for the Anglican Communion

profile.authority: Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, read with the creeds, the early Fathers and reason; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Book of Common Prayer and Ordinal as historic formularies.
profile.salvation: Justification by grace through faith in Christ, with an emphasis on growth in holiness through the Church's common prayer and sacraments.
profile.sacraments: Two dominical sacraments (baptism and Eucharist) and five other 'commonly called sacraments'; views of Eucharistic presence range from Reformed to Anglo-Catholic.
profile.eschatology: The creedal hope of Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed accepted in some traditions of the church.
profile.governance: Episcopal and synodical: two provinces (Canterbury and York), dioceses and a General Synod of bishops, clergy and laity (since 1970); its legislation requires parliamentary approval.
profile.worship: Common prayer: the 1662 Book of Common Prayer and Common Worship (2000); choral evensong and cathedral music.
profile.canon: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).

traditions.status: Active; about one million regular worshippers in the early 2020s, with much wider occasional and cultural affiliation.

traditions.name: Scottish Episcopal Church
traditions.summary: The Anglican church in Scotland, descended from the episcopalian party of the post-Reformation Church of Scotland. When the bishops refused allegiance to William and Mary, episcopacy was abolished (1689) and the church became a disestablished, often Jacobite, minority under penal laws. Its bishops consecrated Samuel Seabury, the first American Anglican bishop, in 1784; its Scottish Communion Office influenced the American Prayer Book.
distinctives: Nonjuring and Jacobite history
Consecration of Samuel Seabury (1784)
Scottish Communion Office with a strong epiclesis
Bishops elect a Primus from among themselves
Approved same-sex marriage in church (2017)

profile.governance: Episcopal and synodical: seven dioceses, a College of Bishops presided over by the Primus, and a General Synod.
profile.worship: Scottish Liturgy (1982) and Scottish Prayer Book tradition.
profile.canon: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).

traditions.status: Active; small minority church in Scotland.

traditions.name: Episcopal Church (United States)
traditions.summary: The first autonomous Anglican province outside the British Isles, organised after the American Revolution with bishops consecrated in Scotland (Seabury, 1784) and England (1787) and a constitution and Prayer Book adopted in Philadelphia (1789). Historically influential far beyond its size, it ordained women priests from 1976, consecrated a partnered gay bishop (2003) and authorised same-sex marriage rites (2015), decisions that strained relations within the Anglican Communion and contributed to the formation of ACNA.
distinctives: Democratic synodical government with lay deputies (General Convention)
Book of Common Prayer (1979)
Dioceses in 17 countries, including Latin America and Taiwan
Progressive positions on women's ordination and sexuality
Historically strong among American elites

profile.governance: General Convention with a House of Bishops and a House of Deputies (clergy and laity); a Presiding Bishop.
profile.worship: Book of Common Prayer (1979) and The Hymnal 1982.
profile.canon: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).

traditions.status: Active; c. 1.5 million baptised members in the early 2020s, declining.

traditions.name: Church of Nigeria (Anglican Communion)
traditions.summary: One of the largest provinces of the Anglican Communion, rooted in the Church Missionary Society missions at Badagry and Abeokuta (1840s) and the ministry of Samuel Ajayi Crowther, consecrated in 1864 as the first African Anglican bishop. A separate province since 1979, it grew rapidly in the 1990s and became a leading voice of theologically conservative global Anglicanism through GAFCON.
distinctives: Very rapid growth and many new dioceses
Leadership in GAFCON (from 2008)
Evangelical and revivalist piety
Ministry in contexts of Christian–Muslim tension in the north

profile.authority: Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, read with the creeds, the early Fathers and reason; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Book of Common Prayer and Ordinal as historic formularies. It affirms the Jerusalem Declaration (2008).
profile.salvation: Justification by grace through faith in Christ, with an emphasis on growth in holiness through the Church's common prayer and sacraments.

profile.eschatology: The creedal hope of Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed accepted in some traditions of the church.
profile.governance: Primate (Archbishop of All Nigeria), fourteen ecclesiastical provinces and a General Synod.
profile.worship: Prayer Book worship in English, Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and other languages, with lively music and dance.
profile.canon: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).

traditions.status: Active; it claims around 18 million members, a figure that is difficult to verify.

traditions.name: Anglican Church of Kenya
traditions.summary: A province of the Anglican Communion rooted in the Church Missionary Society mission begun by Johann Ludwig Krapf at Mombasa in 1844 and deeply shaped by the East African Revival. It became the Church of the Province of Kenya in 1970 and took its present name in 1998. Its leaders have played prominent roles in national public life and in the GAFCON movement.
distinctives: East African Revival (Balokole) heritage
Public engagement on governance and justice
Ordination of women priests (since 1983 in some dioceses)
Active in GAFCON

traditions.name: Church of Uganda
traditions.summary: The Anglican church of Uganda, rooted in the CMS mission at the court of Buganda (1877) and in the witness of the Uganda Martyrs (1885–87). Its piety was transformed by the East African Revival from the 1930s. It became a province in 1961; Archbishop Janani Luwum was murdered in 1977 after protesting abuses under Idi Amin.
distinctives: Uganda Martyrs and Namugongo pilgrimage
Balokole (East African Revival) fellowship
Martyrdom of Archbishop Janani Luwum (1977)
Strong presence in education and health care
Conservative position on sexuality and leadership in GAFCON

traditions.status: Active; about a third of Uganda's population identified as Anglican in the 2014 census.

traditions.name: Anglican Church in North America (ACNA)
traditions.summary: A theologically conservative Anglican church formed in 2009 by dioceses and congregations that left the Episcopal Church and the Anglican Church of Canada, together with older bodies such as the Reformed Episcopal Church (1873). It regards itself as authentically Anglican and is recognised by the GAFCON primates, but it is not a member of the Anglican Communion's formal instruments. It includes evangelical, charismatic and Anglo-Catholic streams, and its dioceses differ on the ordination of women as priests.
distinctives: Jerusalem Declaration (2008) as a confessional basis
Book of Common Prayer (2019)
Church planting emphasis
Recognition by GAFCON rather than Canterbury
Diocesan option on women's ordination to the priesthood
